transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. To start, can you tell me what's been going on that brought you in today?

Hi, Doctor. Thank you so much for seeing me. I, um... I hope I'm explaining this the right way. I don't want to sound like a difficult person or like I'm just complaining, because I'm really not. It's just a bit embarrassing to talk about family matters, I suppose. 

I'm really just here because... well, for months now, I’ve been trying to get people to understand that my husband’s family is quietly messing with our money. And our good name, too. Like, I'll be at work—I do billing—and these little errors will just show up on my accounts out of nowhere. Or someone at our church will suddenly act really funny toward me, just treating me differently for no reason. 

I know it probably sounds a little silly to bring up, and I hope it's okay that I'm telling you this, but... no matter what records anyone pulls up to try and smooth it over or prove otherwise, I just know it all ties back to his family doing this on purpose. I'm just trying to handle it the right way, you know? Does that make sense?
Have you ever heard voices, sounds, or seen things that other people around you didn't seem to notice or hear?

Oh, goodness, no. Um... no, nothing like that at all. I hope I didn't say something to make you think I was... well, imagining things. I promise I'm very level-headed. 

It's really just the actual, physical things happening with my billing accounts and the way people are acting in person. But no voices in my head or seeing things that aren't there. I know some people do struggle with those kinds of things, and my heart goes out to them, but I definitely don't have anything like that going on. Is that... I mean, I hope that's a good thing?

Thinking back over your life, would you say you've generally had a hard time trusting people and often suspected others of trying to deceive or take advantage of you, even before this situation with your husband's family started—say, in friendships, past jobs, or other relationships?

Oh, no. Um... no, definitely not. I've actually always been a very trusting person. Maybe even a little too trusting sometimes? I hope that doesn't make me sound naive or anything. 

Before all this started with my husband's family, I... well, I've always had wonderful friends, and I get along just fine at my jobs. I've always tried to see the best in people, I promise. I've never been the type to hold a grudge or think someone is out to get me. It's really just this one specific situation that's been so difficult and out of the ordinary for me. 

But generally speaking, no, I've never gone around suspecting people of trying to trick me or take advantage of me. Did I answer that right? I just want to make sure I'm giving you what you need.
How many months has it been since you first started noticing these problems with your husband's family and feeling that they were responsible?

Um... well, if I'm remembering right, it's been about nine months now. It all sort of started back when... well, we had a little bit of a disagreement with his family over money and some holiday expectations. You know how stressful the holidays can be for families, I'm sure you hear about that all the time. I really don't want to make them sound like awful people, I know they probably mean well in their own way, but... yes, that's right around when I first started noticing the issues. 

I hope that's the kind of timeline you were looking for? I just want to make sure I'm answering your questions properly and giving you what you need.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits a single, fixed, non-bizarre persecutory delusion (belief that her husband's family is deliberately sabotaging her finances and reputation) persisting for approximately 9 months. She explicitly denies hallucinations (auditory or visual), ruling out schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis with prominent hallucinations. She denies a longstanding pervasive pattern of distrust/suspiciousness predating this specific situation, arguing against paranoid personality disorder. Her affect, insight into social norms, and occupational functioning (still working in billing) appear largely preserved outside the delusional belief system, consistent with delusional disorder rather than schizophrenia, which typically requires broader functional decline and/or other positive symptoms (disorganized speech, negative symptoms, hallucinations). The circumscribed nature of the delusion, absence of bizarre content, and lack of hallucinations or premorbid paranoid traits support a diagnosis of Delusional Disorder, Persecutory Type (F22).
